messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amara is a 47-year-old African American woman who works as a licensed plumber, married and living in a mid-sized city in the Midwest. She came to the clinic after her PCL-5 score of 62 prompted a referral from her primary care physician, though she had been carrying the weight of her childhood for decades before anyone thought to ask about it directly.

Amara grew up in a household where her primary caregiver — her mother — was the source of repeated, severe physical abuse. The beatings were rarely silent. Her mother would call her by her full name before they began, her voice low and deliberate, and the sounds of that household — a belt pulled from its loops, a door slamming, her own name spoken in that particular register — became encoded in her nervous system as signals of inescapable danger. By the time Amara left home at seventeen, she had learned to read sound the way other people read facial expressions: as the first warning of what was coming.

In the years that followed, she built a life through hard work and practical skill. Plumbing suited her — concrete problems, solvable with the right tools, mostly solitary. But the trade also placed her in situations she had not fully anticipated. On job sites, foremen and building inspectors moved through the space with the particular authority of people who could stop her work, critique it, or override her. Amara found herself tensing whenever one of them approached, scanning their body language, cutting conversations short and retreating to her van. She told herself it was professionalism, but over time she began missing bids on larger commercial contracts because they required extended coordination with site supervisors — a pattern that quietly narrowed her income and her professional standing.

The triggers she carries are precise and embodied. Hearing a voice with a particular flat, commanding quality — regardless of gender or context — can pull her back instantly. A coworker once called her name sharply across a job site, and Amara felt her chest lock and her vision narrow before she had consciously registered what had happened. Related sounds — a belt buckle, a door, raised voices in an adjacent room — carry the same charge. These moments do not feel like memories to her; they feel like the present, and they arrive without warning.

When these sensory intrusions strike, they do not resolve cleanly. Instead, they feed directly into what Amara has come to believe about herself: that the abuse happened because of the kind of person she is, that something in her character invited it, that she is fundamentally defective in a way that other people can sense even when she cannot name it. The triggers, in this way, become evidence. Each intrusion seems to confirm the verdict her mother delivered wordlessly through years of violence, and the appraisals deepen with every episode.

The reverse is also true. When Amara sits with the belief that she is broken or blameworthy, the world becomes more threatening — sounds sharpen, voices carry more menace, and she moves through her days in a state of low-grade hypervigilance that makes the next intrusion more likely. The two processes feed each other with a quiet relentlessness she has not been able to interrupt.

What has made this harder is how she has tried to manage it. Amara dwells at length on what was done to her — rehearsing her mother's actions, cataloguing the injustice — and while this feels like it should produce clarity or relief, it instead keeps the appraisals of herself raw and close to the surface, the sense of defectiveness never quite metabolised. Her avoidance of anyone in authority and anything that reminds her of her mother has similarly reinforced rather than loosened the belief that she cannot cope, that the world remains dangerous, that she is the kind of person to whom these things happen. Avoiding perpetrator cues has kept her safe in the short term while confirming, in the long term, that there is something in her that requires protecting from ordinary life.

Amara notes, in a way that stands apart from the rest of her presentation, that nothing in her life feels meaningful anymore — her marriage, her work, her routines all seem to exist at a slight remove from her.

What finally brought her in was her husband's quiet observation that she had not laughed in months. What she is most afraid of is that he is right — and that the reason is not what happened to her, but who she is.
